opening: Saudi Arabia intercepted new Houthi ballistic missiles as the Gulf conflict widened, France deployed 70,000 police for another protest day, and Typhoon Champi battered Taiwan. In Frontiers, Britain committed £600 million to AI security while Moonshot deliberately reduced a new open model’s cyber-offensive capability.

stories.threadTitle: The Iran war and Gulf security
stories.threadSummary: The widening conflict around Iran and its effects on Gulf states, shipping and energy infrastructure.
stories.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts new Houthi ballistic missiles as Gulf front widens
stories.body: The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis toward Taif and Yanbu on Saturday. Civil Defense briefly warned residents in Taif, Yanbu, Mecca and Jeddah before saying the danger had passed. The launches followed a week of attacks and claimed attacks on Saudi airports, energy facilities and government targets, ending the relative calm created by the 2022 truce.
stories.whatChanged: The Houthi campaign continued with confirmed ballistic-missile launches toward western Saudi cities, showing that this week’s attacks were not an isolated burst.
stories.whyMatters: Repeated missile and drone attacks are turning the Yemen front back into an active part of the wider Iran conflict and keep Saudi transport, pilgrimage routes and energy infrastructure exposed to disruption.
stories.uncertainty: Saudi authorities have not confirmed every Houthi claim from earlier in the week, including alleged strikes in Riyadh and Yanbu, and the extent of any physical damage remains unevenly documented.
stories.watchNext: Further Houthi launches, Saudi or coalition retaliation in Yemen, and any confirmed disruption to Saudi oil production, exports or major airports.
keyFacts: The coalition said two ballistic missiles were intercepted on October 24
The missiles were reported headed toward Taif and Yanbu
Warnings also covered Mecca and Jeddah before authorities said the danger had passed
The renewed attacks follow the breakdown of the relative calm established by the 2022 truce

report.heading: Another morning of alerts
paragraphs: Saudi Civil Defense issued brief alerts on Saturday for Taif, Yanbu, Mecca and Jeddah. The Saudi-led coalition later said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward Taif and Yanbu. Authorities lifted the warnings roughly ten minutes later and said the immediate danger had passed.

The interceptions extend a renewed Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia. Earlier in the week the group claimed attacks on targets including Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, the defence ministry in Riyadh and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam. Saudi authorities confirmed deaths after the airport attack but have not confirmed all of the Houthis’ other claims.

report.heading: The Yemen front reopens
paragraphs: The new launches matter because Saudi Arabia and the Houthis had largely avoided direct confrontation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022. That relative calm is now breaking down as the broader US-Israeli war with Iran spreads pressure across the Gulf and Red Sea region.

The immediate military result on Saturday was interception rather than a reported strike. The larger question is whether repeated launches force a sustained Saudi military response in Yemen or produce material disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. Those outcomes would make the renewed front more consequential than the alerts alone.

stories.threadSummary: Protests, riots and the French government's response during the 2026 political and cost-of-living crisis.
stories.title: France deploys 70,000 police as another protest day begins
stories.body: France deployed 70,000 police nationwide on Saturday, 10,000 more than the previous weekend, as demonstrations over living costs and public services returned after last week’s vandalism and looting. Soldiers patrolled the Champs-Élysées, major Paris museums closed and more than 20 metro stations shut. Authorities say radical groups and looters have exploited broader protests; unions and opposition figures argue restrictions risk deepening public anger.
stories.whatChanged: The government moved from announcing tighter protest controls to a nationwide security operation larger than last weekend’s deployment.
stories.whyMatters: The scale of the deployment shows that the unrest has become a sustained test of public order and of the government’s ability to separate peaceful protest from organized violence without escalating the political crisis.
stories.uncertainty: The demonstrations were only beginning by the morning cutoff, so turnout, violence, arrests and the effectiveness of the security plan were not yet known.
stories.watchNext: Whether marches remain peaceful, the number and nature of arrests, and whether restrictions or police tactics become a new focus of the protests.
keyFacts: France mobilised 70,000 police for October 24
That is 10,000 more officers than on October 17
The Louvre, Musée d’Orsay and Paris Opera were among institutions closed
More than 20 Paris metro stations were shut

report.heading: A larger security operation
paragraphs: French security forces spread across Paris and other cities before Saturday’s demonstrations, with Interior Minister Laurent Nunez telling police to respond rapidly to troublemakers and looters. Soldiers from an anti-terrorism unit patrolled the Champs-Élysées while businesses boarded storefronts and major cultural institutions closed.

The 70,000-officer mobilisation exceeded the previous weekend’s deployment by 10,000. Authorities have restricted or redirected demonstrations in several places after vandalism and looting on October 17 raised questions about the government’s ability to maintain order.

report.heading: Two overlapping conflicts
paragraphs: The protest movement is broader than the groups accused of violence. Students, workers and unions have mobilised around living costs and strained public services, while authorities say radical militants and bands of looters have used the gatherings to attack property and police.

That creates a difficult test for the government: preventing a repeat of last weekend without turning restrictions themselves into a grievance. The morning evidence established the scale of preparation, not the outcome of the marches. Saturday’s turnout and conduct will determine whether the crisis is stabilising or entering another cycle of confrontation.

stories.threadSummary: Typhoon Champi’s path and effects across Taiwan, coastal China and Japan.
stories.title: Typhoon Champi leaves one dead and more than 500 injured in Taiwan
stories.body: Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan after briefly reaching super-typhoon strength, killing one person and injuring 527. Coastal gusts reached 227 kph in some areas, power lines and roofs were damaged, and hundreds of flights were cancelled. The storm weakened after looping near Taiwan’s northeast coast and was moving north toward the Chinese coast, with southern Japan later on its forecast track.
stories.whatChanged: Champi’s forecast threat became a documented impact event in Taiwan, with a death, hundreds of injuries, major power disruption and transport cancellations.
stories.whyMatters: The storm is weakening but remains a multi-country hazard as its track shifts north, while Taiwan begins recovery from unusually strong coastal winds and widespread disruption.
stories.uncertainty: Its exact track and intensity over the next several days remain forecast-dependent; China was preparing for the storm even though landfall there was not expected in the morning forecast.
stories.watchNext: Champi’s path near China’s Zhejiang coast and southern Japan, additional rainfall or coastal damage, and restoration of power and transport in Taiwan.
keyFacts: Taiwan reported one death and 527 injuries
Coastal gusts reached 227 kph in some areas
More than 288,000 households lost power at some point
259 flights were cancelled Saturday after much larger disruption Friday

report.heading: The storm clips Taiwan
paragraphs: Champi passed close to Taiwan’s northeastern coast early Saturday after being one of the strongest Pacific storms of the year. The storm made an unusual loop offshore near Yilan before turning north. Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration said it was weakening, with gusts near the centre around 126 kph, but some coastal stations recorded much stronger gusts as it passed.

A man was swept away by waves near Liuqiu Island, and authorities reported 527 injuries. Power lines, trees and roofs were damaged. More than 288,000 households lost electricity at some point, although most service had been restored by the morning.

report.heading: The track turns north
paragraphs: Transport remained heavily affected, with 259 flights cancelled Saturday after nearly 1,000 cancellations on Friday. Northern and central areas, including Taipei, kept schools and offices closed for a second day.

The storm was moving toward China’s Zhejiang coast, where authorities mobilised emergency resources and brought fishing vessels back to harbour, though the forecast did not call for a Chinese landfall. Southern Japan remained farther along the projected path. The key uncertainty is how quickly Champi weakens as it moves north.

stories.threadSummary: Political, economic and security ties between North Korea and China.
stories.title: Kim Jong Un crosses new bridge into China for Dandong visit
stories.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un entered China through the newly opened New Yalu River Bridge and was met in Dandong by Chinese Premier Li Qiang, according to South Korean officials. The bridge opened this month after years of delay and is expected to expand heavy freight between the two countries. Kim was expected to return the same day rather than continue to Beijing.
stories.whatChanged: Kim personally used the new cross-border bridge during a high-level visit, underscoring the renewed economic and political connection between Pyongyang and Beijing.

sources.title: North Korea's Kim Jong Un visits China via Dandong bridge, South Korean official says

stories.threadSummary: Brazil’s presidential campaign and runoff between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro.
stories.title: Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro clash in final debate before Brazil runoff
stories.body: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro traded attacks over living costs, taxes and corruption in their final televised debate before Sunday’s presidential runoff. Polls showed a close race after Bolsonaro led the first round. Campaign advertising restrictions took effect Saturday, leaving the debate as one of the final major national campaign moments.
stories.whatChanged: Brazil’s closely fought presidential race entered its final weekend after the candidates’ last televised confrontation.

sources.title: Bolsonaro and Lula clash on living costs, corruption in final Brazil election debate

stories.threadSummary: Russia's war on Ukraine, the diplomacy around it and its spillover into European security.
stories.title: Kyiv says Russia is intensifying attacks on Ukraine’s digital infrastructure
stories.body: Ukraine’s prime minister said Russian attacks on digital infrastructure are accelerating alongside strikes on energy systems, including attacks on 10 Kyiv data centres last month. He also said AI-assisted cyberattacks against government and business systems are increasing. The claims come as Ukraine faces continued pressure on physical infrastructure and shortages in some air-defence capabilities.
stories.whatChanged: Ukraine is now describing data centres and government information systems as a rapidly intensifying front in Russia’s infrastructure campaign.

sources.title: Russia steps up attacks on Ukraine's digital infrastructure, Kyiv says

stories.threadTitle: The Iran war and global energy shock
stories.threadSummary: How the Iran war is reshaping energy prices, supply routes and government policy.
stories.title: Trump invokes Defense Production Act to expand US oil and refining capacity
stories.body: President Donald Trump declared petroleum production, refining and related infrastructure essential to national defence, opening a route for federal financial incentives under the Defense Production Act. The memo named no projects, but follows sharp increases in crude and diesel prices during the Iran war and an earlier plan to support refinery expansion in Texas.
stories.whatChanged: Washington is moving from calls for more domestic energy production to using national-defence financing authority to support oil, refining, pipelines and fuel storage.

sources.title: Trump invokes Cold War-era Defense Production Act for oil production, refining

stories.threadSummary: Government and industry efforts to measure and reduce security risks from increasingly capable AI systems.
stories.title: Britain commits £600 million to AI security and biosecurity programmes
stories.body: Britain set out roughly £600 million in funding focused on security and health risks from artificial intelligence. The largest component is a new biosecurity initiative, including £100 million for a laboratory using AI to detect biological threats and £65 million to develop countermeasures against pathogens. The package marks a shift from AI-safety institutions built mainly around evaluation toward substantial physical and research infrastructure.
stories.whatChanged: The UK moved from primarily evaluating advanced-model risks to funding a large security programme that includes laboratories and biological countermeasure development.
stories.whyMatters: AI risk policy is beginning to produce concrete national-security infrastructure, especially around the possibility that AI could amplify biological threats.
stories.uncertainty: Funding announcements do not establish that the planned systems will detect threats effectively, and implementation details and timelines vary across the programme.
stories.watchNext: How the biosecurity laboratory is structured, what threat models it evaluates, and whether independent evidence emerges that the funded countermeasures improve preparedness.
stories.hook: AI safety policy is moving from model tests into laboratories and national-security infrastructure.
keyFacts: The UK package totals about £600 million ($800 million)
£100 million is allocated for a laboratory using AI to detect biological threats
£65 million is allocated to pathogen countermeasure development
The funding was announced October 24

report.heading: From evaluation to infrastructure
paragraphs: The British government announced around £600 million of funding on Saturday aimed largely at health and security threats associated with artificial intelligence. A major biosecurity component includes £100 million for a laboratory intended to use AI to detect biological threats and £65 million for work on countermeasures against pathogens.

The package is notable because advanced-AI safety policy has often centred on model evaluation, standards and governance. Britain is now pairing that work with physical laboratories and research programmes intended to strengthen defenses against threats that AI could help create or accelerate.

report.heading: What the announcement does not show
paragraphs: The funding itself is evidence of a policy commitment, not of technical effectiveness. Reuters’ report describes planned programmes and allocations; it does not establish that AI-based detection will reliably identify novel biological threats or that the countermeasures will work against future pathogens.

The important next evidence will come from implementation: laboratory design, access rules, evaluation methods and demonstrated performance. The programme nevertheless changes the scale of Britain’s response by putting hundreds of millions of pounds behind AI-related security rather than treating it mainly as a regulatory question.

stories.threadSummary: How increasingly capable AI systems are changing vulnerability discovery, exploitation and software defence.
stories.title: Moonshot deliberately reduces hacking ability in new open-weight Kimi model
stories.body: Chinese AI developer Moonshot said it removed cyber-offensive training data and reinforcement-learning environments from Kimi K3.1 Pro before releasing its weights, while trying to preserve general coding performance. On Moonshot’s own controlled benchmark, the modified model scored 81.0% on vulnerability finding and exploitation versus 90.5% for an unfiltered version. The results have not been independently verified.
stories.whatChanged: A major open-model developer has explicitly traded away some measured cyber capability before releasing model weights, rather than relying only on post-release safeguards.
stories.whyMatters: Open weights are difficult to monitor or revoke after release, so capability reduction during training may become an important safety strategy if it can preserve useful coding performance.
stories.uncertainty: The benchmark is Moonshot’s own and has not been independently replicated; it is unclear how well the measured reduction transfers to real-world offensive cyber tasks.
stories.watchNext: Independent evaluations after the November 4 weight release, whether the capability gap persists outside Moonshot’s benchmark, and whether other open-model developers adopt similar training exclusions.
stories.hook: An open-model lab is testing whether dangerous capability can be reduced before weights become impossible to recall.
keyFacts: Moonshot plans to release Kimi K3.1 Pro weights on November 4
The company removed cyber-related data from training and reinforcement-learning environments
Moonshot reported an 81.0% cyber benchmark score for the modified model versus 90.5% for an unfiltered version
The reported benchmark results have not been independently verified

report.heading: A pre-release intervention
paragraphs: Moonshot said it intentionally reduced the offensive cybersecurity capability of Kimi K3.1 Pro before a planned November 4 open-weight release. The company removed cyber-related material from parts of the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments while attempting to retain broader software-development ability.

On an internal controlled benchmark for finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, Moonshot reported that the modified model scored 81.0%, compared with 90.5% for a similar unfiltered version. The modified system still exceeded its predecessor, according to the company. Reuters noted that the results have not been independently verified.

report.heading: Why open weights change the safety problem
paragraphs: Hosted models can be monitored, filtered or withdrawn by their operators. Once model weights are broadly distributed, those controls become much weaker. That makes pre-release capability shaping potentially more important for open models, especially for skills that can be used both to defend and attack software.

The central unresolved question is whether Moonshot has reduced harmful capability in a robust way or mainly changed performance on its own test. Independent evaluation after release will matter, as will evidence about whether general coding quality was genuinely preserved. The experiment is therefore significant as a safety strategy, not yet as proof that the strategy works.

stories.threadSummary: Sudan's conflict, displacement and worsening food emergency.
stories.title: Sudan’s drought and war are converging into a deeper food emergency
stories.body: Sudan’s weakest July-to-September rainfall in more than three decades is still threatening the coming harvest as war and aid shortages leave millions acutely hungry. The World Food Programme expects drought to push hundreds of thousands more people into severe hunger by year-end. A separate drone strike this week in Abyei, on a market tied to fuel routes serving the RSF, also showed the conflict spilling into neighboring territory.
stories.whatChanged: The food crisis remains a priority because the expected harvest is weakening just as aid resources shrink and the war’s supply networks spread instability beyond Sudan.
stories.whyMatters: A failed harvest removes one of the few remaining buffers for communities already hit by displacement, inflation and reduced humanitarian rations.
stories.uncertainty: The IPC is still updating national hunger estimates, and responsibility for the deadly Abyei strike remains disputed.
stories.watchNext: The next IPC assessment, actual November-December harvest yields, aid funding and any further cross-border spillover around Abyei.
keyFacts: July-September rainfall was Sudan’s lowest in more than three decades
WFP forecasts drought could add 350,000 people to severe hunger by year-end
A strike on Amiet market in Abyei killed more than 150 people according to Reuters reporting
Responsibility for the Abyei strike remains unclear

report.heading: The harvest remains the central risk
paragraphs: Drought has damaged crops and pasture across Sudan after the weakest peak rainy season in more than three decades. That shock comes after years of war disrupted farming, markets and humanitarian access. The World Food Programme expects drought alone to add hundreds of thousands of people to severe-hunger totals by the end of the year.

The importance of the next harvest is therefore unusually high. If production disappoints while aid agencies continue ration cuts, conflict-affected areas will have fewer ways to absorb another food-price or access shock.

report.heading: The war reaches beyond Sudan
paragraphs: A drone strike this week on Amiet market in Abyei, the disputed territory between Sudan and South Sudan, killed more than 150 people. Reuters reporting found that the market had become part of a fuel supply network serving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, illustrating how the war’s logistics extend into neighbouring territory.

Sudan’s government denied involvement in the strike, while South Sudan’s account evolved and the circumstances remain unclear. The episode matters less as a settled attribution than as evidence that the conflict’s supply chains and violence are increasingly entangling communities outside Sudan’s core battle zones.

briefs.title: El Niño rains batter countries from Mexico to Chile
briefs.text: Flooding, erosion and severe weather have hit several Latin American countries. Paraguay and Argentina reported deaths and evacuations, Mexico saw coastal structural damage, and Peru announced financial and tax support for affected businesses.

briefs.text: Russia and Ukraine completed another prisoner exchange after talks involving US negotiators. Ukraine said nine civilians were among those returning, while Russia said seven Russian civilians were returned.

africa.summary: Sudan’s drought and war remain the continent’s largest humanitarian emergency, while the expanding Ebola outbreak has now produced a second death in Kenya.

briefs.title: Kenya reports second Ebola death
briefs.text: Kenya reported a second Ebola death, a 65-year-old woman who was a close contact of the country’s first confirmed patient. Nine cases have been confirmed in Kenya; authorities say they have traced 135 contacts and have not found evidence of community transmission.
